data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a critical methodological rule: we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it offers the most informative potential falsifier for the next test, thereby maximizing the growth of knowledge even if the theory is ultimately false.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent acts on the theory believing it is likely to succeed in novel domains based on past performance, they have smuggled in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference cannot distinguish between a theory that survived due to lenient tests versus severe tests, the defense fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'aim of truth' itself requires an inductive assumption that nature is uniform enough for truth-seeking to be viable, the circle remains unbroken.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'Critical Preferential Selection': Action is guided by the theory that currently best solves the problem at hand (has the highest verisimilitude content relative to known errors), not because it is probable to be true, but because it is the most rationally criticizable object available. Preference is a decision to expose the strongest available conjecture to new risks, which is the engine of scientific progress. This avoids induction by treating the preference as a voluntary commitment to the aim of truth-seeking rather than a logical derivation of safety.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
